consensus_summary: The shared consensus identifies “works of the law” as deeds associated with observance of the Mosaic Torah, especially when treated as a basis for justification. It also recognizes substantial disagreement over whether these are the whole Torah, boundary markers, ceremonial requirements, or merit-seeking works more generally.
book_summary: The book treats the phrase as context-dependent deeds considered in relation to law, not as a fixed class or a synonym for obedience. Its constant element is the invalid claim that such deeds can purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or put God in debt.
consensus_core_identification: Deeds associated with Mosaic-law observance that cannot serve as the basis of justification before God.
book_core_identification: Contextually identified deeds related to law whose claimed efficacy as the purchase price of divine standing or blessing is denied.
boundary_disagreement: The book broadens the ordinary identification beyond deeds that actually obey the Mosaic Torah. It includes context-specific circumcision-party applications and potentially unnamed deeds merely considered under a law-based claim, while refusing to define one stable class of acts. Obedient Torah deeds remain included but no longer define the phrase’s full extension.
material_contradiction: There is no contradiction at the shared center: both readings connect the deeds with law and deny their power to justify. The material difference is that the predominant consensus tends to identify the acts by their Torah-observant character, whereas the book makes the rejected claim made for contextually variable acts the phrase’s stable feature.
rationale: This is REFINED rather than MATCH because the book materially changes how cases are classified: “works of the law” is not a fixed set of Mosaic-law observances but a contextual category unified by an invalid instrumental claim. It is not DIVERGENT because it retains the consensus’s central law-related referent and justification contrast, and the consensus itself already contains alternatives involving boundary markers and particular halakhic applications.
strongest_objection: The printed texts strongly support the denial that works of the law justify or produce the Spirit, but they do not by themselves establish that the phrase lacks a stable Torah-observance referent. Galatians 3:10’s appeal to doing everything written in the law may instead suggest that actual Torah performance remains integral to the phrase’s meaning.
